verified_ref: Yoga Vasishtha 2.15.11 (Mumukshu-vyavahara-prakarana, sarga 15 'santosha-nirupana'). Same number in the Nirnaya Sagar text with Anandabodhendra's Tatparya-prakasha (Pansikar 1937), sa.wikisource and Mitra 1891 (Mumukshu ch. XV v. 11).
attribution_note: Vasishtha to Rama, in his chapter on contentment, as stated.
translation_note: Accurate. 'Akinchana' is literally 'one who has nothing'; 'adhi-vyadhi' is mental and bodily affliction. Mitra reads the same way (a poor man enjoys sovereign-like happiness if free of disease and anxiety and content).
context: Vasishtha has named four 'gatekeepers' of freedom and gives this chapter to the third, contentment. Just before, he says a mind without contentment cannot reflect knowledge, like a tarnished mirror (v.9). Right after, he defines the contented person as one who does not crave what has not come and enjoys what does come, in its order (v.12).

key_terms.sense: one who owns nothing, the poor
tastes the happiness of an emperor
free of mental and bodily affliction

core_teaching: Happiness depends on the state of the mind more than on possessions: a content, untroubled mind is already rich. The chapter defines contentment as not craving the unobtained and receiving what comes evenly.

commentaries.who: Anandabodhendra Sarasvati, Tatparya-prakasha (Sanskrit commentary)
commentaries.gist: Passes over v.11 without separate comment, but glosses the chapter: contentment is called the highest good because in it lasting freedom from sorrow is tasted; v.3 notes that even in poverty or separation a contented mind is not lost.

commentaries.who: Context of the chapter (Mitra tr. 1891, Mumukshu ch. XV)
commentaries.gist: Surrounding verses say the content regard sovereignty as rotten straw, that great fortunes wait on a contented mind like servants on a king, and that contentment settles anxieties as rain settles dust.

practical_reading: Before measuring your life by what you lack, check whether the mind is at peace with what is here; a settled mind turns a modest life into a rich one.
misreadings: Not a claim that poverty is fine or that material need is imaginary
Not an instruction to stop working or striving; v.14 of the same chapter asks for 'manly effort' to drop craving
cautions: For a reader in real financial hardship or illness this can sound like 'just be content'; the verse itself says freedom from adhi and vyadhi is part of the condition
speaks_to: someone downsizing or living simply by choice
not_for: someone struggling to pay for food, rent or treatment
acute illness (the verse assumes freedom from vyadhi)

verified_ref: Yoga Vasishtha 2.15.19 (Mumukshu, sarga 15). Same in Nirnaya Sagar/TP, sa.wikisource; Mitra 1891 Mumukshu XV v.19.
attribution_note: Vasishtha to Rama.
translation_note: Fair. The printed Sanskrit (and our data) reads 'vakram', which literally means 'crooked'; the sense requires 'vaktram' (face), and Mitra translates 'countenance'. Likely an old typographic form; worth correcting the Sanskrit to वक्त्रं if a better edition confirms. 'Samata' is evenness/equanimity; the commentator glosses it as an even, non-discriminating view everywhere that comes from contentment.
context: Closing verses of the chapter on contentment. Before it, the contented person is said to shine like the full moon by pure conduct (v.18). After it, the chapter ends saying even celestials and great sages bow to the one adorned with equanimity (v.20); the next chapter turns to good company.
core_teaching: An even, contented person is a joy to others; the sight of such calm gives people more delight than accumulated money gives its owner.

commentaries.who: Anandabodhendra Sarasvati, Tatparya-prakasha
commentaries.gist: Samata here means an even-minded view toward everything, born of contentment.

commentaries.who: Context of the chapter (Mitra tr. 1891, Mumukshu ch. XV)
commentaries.gist: Mitra renders it as more delight from seeing the placid face of a contented person than from piling up wealth; v.20 says the even-minded are honoured by gods and sages.

practical_reading: Your calm is a gift to the people around you; a steady, unhurried presence at home or work often matters more to them than what you earn or buy.
misreadings: Not about physical good looks
Not a rule that one must look cheerful all the time
cautions: Could press someone who feels depressed to 'put on a calm face'; it praises inner evenness, not masking
speaks_to: parents or leaders who feel they must provide more and more
someone realising their mood shapes the household
not_for: someone in depression being told to appear serene
someone grieving

verified_ref: Yoga Vasishtha 2.16.3 (Mumukshu, sarga 16, on sadhu-samagama). Same in Nirnaya Sagar/TP, sa.wikisource; Mitra 1891 Mumukshu XVI v.3.
attribution_note: Vasishtha to Rama.
translation_note: Accurate. Two readings of 'shunya' are attested: the commentator glosses it as a place empty of kin and wealth that becomes filled; Mitra reads 'solitude seems like company'. 'Mṛti' is death. (The OCR of the 1937 print is blurred at this word, but wikisource and Mitra both support 'mṛti'.)
context: Opening of the chapter on the fourth gatekeeper, good company. Vasishtha has just said such company helps people everywhere in crossing worldly life and grows the flower of discernment (vv.1-2). After this he calls it frost on the lotus-pond of calamity and the cutter of the tree of ignorance (vv.4-5), and says it should not be given up even in the worst plight (v.8).

key_terms.sense: even death becomes like a festival

core_teaching: The company of the wise changes how life's hardest facts appear: loneliness, loss and even death lose their sting when seen in their light.

commentaries.who: Anandabodhendra Sarasvati, Tatparya-prakasha
commentaries.gist: 'Empty' means empty of relatives and wealth, a place of sorrow; in the company of the wise it becomes as if filled.

commentaries.who: Context of the chapter (Mitra tr. 1891, Mumukshu ch. XVI)
commentaries.gist: Mitra: the society of the learned makes solitude feel like company, death like a festivity, difficulty like ease; v.17 adds that this 'medicine' allays the afflictions of poverty and death.

practical_reading: When life feels empty or frightening, seek out people whose understanding steadies you, a teacher, a wise friend, a satsang; how you see your situation changes in their presence.
misreadings: Not a claim that death is literally happy or that loss should be celebrated
Not 'only spiritual people are worth knowing'
cautions: 'Death feels like a festival' can wound someone in fresh grief; use only with care and framing about perspective, not about the loss itself
speaks_to: loneliness after a move or breakup
someone isolating in a hard time
value of a support group or satsang
not_for: the first days after a death
someone who has no access to good company and may feel blamed

verified_ref: Yoga Vasishtha 2.16.19 (Mumukshu, sarga 16). Same in Nirnaya Sagar/TP, sa.wikisource; Mitra 1891 Mumukshu XVI v.19.
attribution_note: Vasishtha to Rama; summary of the four gatekeepers named in v.18.
translation_note: Accurate. 'Gati' can be path or refuge/destination; Mitra gives 'the right course'. 'Vichara' is inquiry or reasoned reflection; 'shama' is calm, quietude.
context: Vasishtha has praised good company at length. In v.18 he lists the four means of crossing worldly life (contentment, good company, inquiry, calm); this verse ranks each as the highest of its kind. He goes on to say these four are the pure means to break bondage (v.20) and that practising one brings the rest (vv.21-22).

key_terms.sense: good company is the best path/refuge

core_teaching: Four inner resources, contentment, good company, inquiry and calm, are the real wealth, path, knowledge and joy; each is described as supreme by naming it after what it yields.

commentaries.who: Anandabodhendra Sarasvati, Tatparya-prakasha
commentaries.gist: In each phrase the result is figuratively identified with its means: contentment is 'gain' because it yields what gain is sought for, and so on for all four.

commentaries.who: Context of the chapter (Mitra tr. 1891, Mumukshu ch. XVI)
commentaries.gist: Mitra: contentment the best gain, good company the right course, reasoning the true knowledge, quietism the highest bliss; whoever practises these crosses the world's sea (v.20).

practical_reading: A simple four-part check for a day: have I been content, did I spend time with good people, did I think clearly about what matters, did I find some calm?
misreadings: Not a dismissal of material gain or formal learning; it ranks inner goods above them
not_for: acute crisis where a list of ideals may feel abstract

verified_ref: Yoga Vasishtha 2.16.32 (Mumukshu, sarga 16). Same in Nirnaya Sagar/TP, sa.wikisource; Mitra 1891 Mumukshu XVI v.32.
attribution_note: Vasishtha to Rama.
translation_note: Accurate. Our 'line' ('One good habit feeds the others') is a fair modern paraphrase; the verse speaks of virtues (guna) and faults (dosha), not habits as such.
context: Having said that practising any one of the four gatekeepers brings the others, Vasishtha urges Rama to win the mind by effort and grow at least one, 'grinding teeth on teeth' if need be (vv.27-30). Just before this verse he says that once one fruitful virtue gains strength, the faults of the mind wane (v.31). After it he pictures desire as a river with good and bad banks that you can steer by effort (vv.33-34).
core_teaching: Qualities compound: strengthening one virtue strengthens the others and weakens faults, while letting one fault grow feeds the rest and erodes virtues. So start with one.

commentaries.who: Anandabodhendra Sarasvati, Tatparya-prakasha
commentaries.gist: Of two mutually opposed things, when one grows its whole kind grows with it; the commentator calls this a well-known principle.

commentaries.who: Context of the chapter (Mitra tr. 1891, Mumukshu ch. XVI)
commentaries.gist: Mitra: cultivating virtues makes them grow and suppresses vice, while fostering vice increases vices and suppresses good qualities; the next verse likens desire to a river steered between good and bad banks.

practical_reading: Pick one small good practice and keep it; it tends to pull others along. Equally, notice which single bad pattern is quietly dragging the rest down.
misreadings: Not a threat that one lapse ruins everything
Not a claim that people are simply good or bad
cautions: A reader with harsh self-judgment may read the second half as doom; stress the first half and the chapter's call to start with one
speaks_to: starting a turnaround after a slump
someone overwhelmed by trying to fix everything at once
not_for: someone in shame spirals who may hear only 'faults multiply'

verified_ref: Yoga Vasishtha 3.16.24 (Utpatti-prakarana, sarga 16, Lilopakhyana: 'the queen's lament'). Same number in Nirnaya Sagar/TP, sa.wikisource; Mitra 1891 Utpatti ch. XVI v.24.
attribution_note: Spoken by the brahmins (vipra ucuh) to Queen Lila, inside Vasishtha's narration to Rama. Correct.
translation_note: Accurate. 'Siddha-siddhayah' are the attainments of the perfected; 'yama' is discipline/restraint. The commentator notes she was asking about immortality for her husband and herself.
context: Queen Lila, devoted to King Padma, fears losing him and calls learned brahmins to ask how a person can escape death (vv.19-23). They answer with this verse. She then resolves that if he dies first, his soul should not leave the palace, and begins long worship of the goddess Sarasvati, who grants her boons (vv.25-41).
core_teaching: Effort and devotion can achieve a great deal, but no practice wins freedom from bodily death; the story then moves Lila from this fear toward understanding.

commentaries.who: Anandabodhendra Sarasvati, Tatparya-prakasha
commentaries.gist: Glosses the request as immortality for both her husband and herself, and the following verses as her private reflection on the brahmins' answer.

commentaries.who: Context of the story (Mitra tr. 1891, Utpatti ch. XVI)
commentaries.gist: Mitra: holy men may succeed in everything by austerity, prayer and rites, but none attains immortality here; Lila, fearing her lord's death, then turns to worship of Sarasvati.

practical_reading: Love that tries to guarantee a loved one will never die meets a hard limit; the story invites shifting from controlling death to understanding life, while still caring fully.
misreadings: Not fatalism about medical care
Not a dismissal of prayer or discipline; it names one thing they cannot do
cautions: Mentions death directly; for someone with a seriously ill partner or parent it can land as hopelessness unless framed as the start of Lila's journey
speaks_to: anticipatory fear of losing a spouse or parent
new parents' fear for a child's safety
not_for: someone currently at a deathbed
fresh bereavement (use the later teaching of the story instead)

verified_ref: Yoga Vasishtha 3.16.50, last verse of Utpatti sarga 16. Same in Nirnaya Sagar/TP, sa.wikisource; Mitra 1891 Utpatti ch. XVI v.50.
attribution_note: Narrative verse in Vasishtha's telling to Rama. Our 'prasang' field is null for this verse (data gap); it belongs to the Lila story (same prasang as yv.3.16.24).
translation_note: Accurate. 'Akasha-bhava' is 'born of the sky'; the commentator reads it as 'bodiless'. 'Anvakampata' is 'felt compassion for'; the commentator says its fruit is consolation.
context: After Sarasvati's boons, time passes and King Padma dies. Lila wastes with grief: pale, mute, about to die like a female chakravaka parted from its mate (vv.44-49). This verse closes the chapter. In the next, Sarasvati tells her to cover the body with flowers, promises he will return, and begins teaching her about the nature of worlds and death.

key_terms.sense: a small fish gasping as its pond dries

core_teaching: Grace meets grief first with compassion, like first rain reaching a stranded fish; the teaching that follows comes only after that.

commentaries.who: Anandabodhendra Sarasvati, Tatparya-prakasha
commentaries.gist: Sarasvati is compassionate because Lila had worshipped her over many births, and her compassion culminates in giving knowledge of truth; 'compassion' here implies consolation as its fruit.

commentaries.who: Context of the story (Mitra tr. 1891, Utpatti ch. XVI-XVII)
commentaries.gist: Mitra: the goddess took pity on her excess of grief, like the first shower on dying fishes in a drying pond; ch. XVII opens with Sarasvati's practical comfort before any doctrine.

practical_reading: When someone is crushed by loss, the first response is compassion and presence; explanations can wait. If you are the one grieving, help may come before understanding does.
misreadings: Not a promise that the dead return (Lila's story uses this to teach about illusion and consciousness)
cautions: Describes a widow near death from grief; tender for the newly bereaved but should not hint at the story's later 'restoration' as a promise
speaks_to: carers wanting to know how to sit with someone grieving
not_for: someone who will read the story's sequel as 'your loved one will come back'
research_note: prasang is null in our data; should be linked to the Lila prasang.

verified_ref: Yoga Vasishtha 5.9.46-47 (Upashama-prakarana, sarga 9, Janaka's reflection). Same in Nirnaya Sagar/TP and sa.wikisource; Mitra 1891 Upashama ch. IX vv.46-47.
attribution_note: Janaka speaking to himself (v.45 addresses his own mind in the second person: 'why do you crave?'), within Vasishtha's narration. Correct.
translation_note: Good. 'Sammata' is 'esteemed, held dear'; 'maharambha' is 'grand in its beginnings / costly to start'. The commentator reads fortunes as hard to win, hard to guard and sure to go, hence calamities; and misfortunes such as poverty or loss of kin or kingdom as fortunes when they lead to good company, pilgrimage, austerity and awakening, i.e. to dispassion. So 'if the mind accepts them' is close, but the point is that hardship becomes wealth when it turns one inward.
context: Janaka, shaken by the Siddhas' songs, sits alone and reviews his life: heavenly rewards are short-lived, good is mixed with evil, beings far greater than he have perished (vv.38-45). He then says prized fortunes are calamities and accepted adversities are fortunes (46-47), that the world is a play of the mind (48) and that calling things 'mine' is a strange new script (48).

key_terms.sense: fortunes held dear by the mind

core_teaching: Whether something is a fortune or a calamity depends on how the mind holds it: clung-to wealth breeds trouble, while hardship that turns one toward wisdom becomes real wealth.

commentaries.who: Anandabodhendra Sarasvati, Tatparya-prakasha
commentaries.gist: Varied riches (jewels, elephants, wealth, family) are won with great effort, painful to protect and bound to perish, so they are calamities; poverty, loss of kin or kingdom become fortunes if they lead to good company, austerity and awakening.

commentaries.who: Context of the soliloquy (Mitra tr. 1891, Upashama ch. IX)
commentaries.gist: Mitra: prosperity is mere vexation that proves a calamity, while feared adversities may become true prosperity by freeing one from worldly entanglement.

practical_reading: Look at what you are proudest of and what you most resent: the first may be costing you peace, and the second may be pushing you toward something better.
misreadings: Not a reason to romanticise poverty or loss
Not a rule against enjoying success; the problem is the mind's clinging
cautions: Telling someone in acute hardship that it is 'really a fortune' can feel dismissive; offer as a later reflection, not first comfort
speaks_to: a setback that redirected a career or life
job loss or failure seen in hindsight
not_for: the immediate aftermath of a loss or disaster
someone in poverty being told to be grateful
research_note: id is yv.5.9.46 but the text spans 46-47.

verified_ref: Yoga Vasishtha 5.9.59 (Upashama, sarga 9). Same in Nirnaya Sagar/TP and sa.wikisource; Mitra 1891 Upashama ch. IX v.59.
attribution_note: Janaka to himself. But our 'setting' ('decides to stop replaying his losses') misframes it: in context the lament is not over lost people or things.
translation_note: Literal translation fine. Context changes the meaning: the cries 'I am slain, ruined, dead' are Janaka's past lament over his own bondage, and the next verse says he has now seen the 'thief of the self', the mind, that had long 'slain' him. The commentator glosses: what I mourned again and again before is over; now I do not grieve. Mitra reads it as ceasing to lament the loss of his soul. It is an awakening verse, not a bereavement verse.
context: Janaka has realised the world tree grows from the mind and resolves to stop being fooled by appearances (vv.55-58). Here he ends his repeated self-pity. Next he declares 'I am awake, I am glad, I have seen the thief, the mind' (v.60) and resolves to rest in the Self. Then his doorkeeper arrives (ch.10).

key_terms.sense: I am struck down, ruined, dead

core_teaching: Once one sees that the mind itself was the source of feeling lost, repeated self-lament can be set down; the verse marks a turning from despair to awakening.

commentaries.who: Anandabodhendra Sarasvati, Tatparya-prakasha
commentaries.gist: Whatever I lamented over and over before is finished; from now on I do not grieve.

commentaries.who: Context of the soliloquy (Mitra tr. 1891, Upashama ch. IX)
commentaries.gist: Mitra: he had wailed long over the depravity and loss of his soul and now ceases, knowing he is not utterly lost; next he finds the robber of his soul to be his own mind.

practical_reading: When you notice an old loop of 'I'm finished, I'm ruined', you can name it and set it down; often the voice saying it is the problem, not the facts.
misreadings: Not 'stop grieving the dead'
Not a command to suppress tears
cautions: Do not use on Day 1 of a grief plan; in context it is about self-pity and spiritual despair, not mourning a person
Our setting line should be revised from 'replaying his losses' to 'his old cries of being lost'
speaks_to: a moment of resolve to change the inner narrative
not_for: recent bereavement
someone who has not yet been allowed to grieve

verified_ref: Yoga Vasishtha 5.10.9 (Upashama, sarga 10, 'Janaka's resolve'). Same in Nirnaya Sagar/TP and sa.wikisource; Mitra 1891 Upashama ch. X v.9.
attribution_note: The pratihara (chamberlain/doorkeeper) to Janaka. Correct.
translation_note: Accurate. 'Niyatam karyam' is the fixed/appointed duty (the day's rites and business); 'kalam ativartante' is 'let the time pass by'.
context: As Janaka sits absorbed, his chamberlain enters and lists the waiting baths, worship, brahmins and meals (vv.2-8), ending with this call. Important: Janaka does not rise at once. He keeps reflecting, calls the kingdom fleeting and resolves to stay apart (vv.10-12; Mitra's longer chapter continues his reasoning). Only at the start of ch.11 does he rise and do his duties without the sense of being the doer.

key_terms.sense: they do not let the time slip past
the great, in their own duties

core_teaching: The ordinary call of duty and punctuality; in the story it tests Janaka's insight, which he then carries back into his daily work.

commentaries.who: Context of the chapter (Mitra tr. 1891, Upashama ch. X)
commentaries.gist: Mitra: rise and do the prescribed duties, since it does not become the best of men to be late; yet the king stayed in meditation, calling royalty transitory, before concluding his inner self is unaffected by action.

commentaries.who: Context of the next chapter (Mitra tr. 1891, Upashama ch. XI)
commentaries.gist: Mitra: having thought it through, Janaka rose for his daily rites without the sense of agency, doing duties as they came without concern for reward.

practical_reading: Insight does not cancel the day's work; get up and do what is due, but let the doing come from a settled mind.
misreadings: Not 'busyness is virtue'
Not that reflection is a waste of time; Janaka's pause is what changes how he works
cautions: Our note implies Janaka returns to work straight after this call; in the text he first keeps reflecting and only rises in ch.11
speaks_to: getting back to work after a period of withdrawal
not_for: someone exhausted or ill who needs rest
burnout where 'get up and do it' is the wrong message
research_note: Anandabodhendra's commentary on 5.10.9 could not be isolated in the OCR; the two notes are from Mitra's text of chs. X and XI.

verified_ref: Yoga Vasishtha 5.12.14 (Upashama, sarga 12). Same in Nirnaya Sagar/TP and sa.wikisource; Mitra 1891 Upashama ch. XII v.14.
attribution_note: Vasishtha describing the liberated Janaka. Correct.
translation_note: Accurate. 'Anusandhatte' is 'plans toward / keeps fixing on'; 'nimesha' is 'blink, moment'; 'hasann eva' is 'just smiling'. Note our 'line' turns a description into an instruction ('Don't chase...'), which is fine for a reading.
context: After his reflection Janaka becomes a jivanmukta who rules the Videhas, untouched by joy or sorrow (vv.9-12), his mental impressions dissolved as in deep sleep (v.13). This verse describes his relation to time. Vasishtha then draws the lesson: Janaka gained this by his own inquiry, not by a guru, scripture or merit alone, and praises prajna (vv.15-27).

key_terms.sense: does not fix on the future
does not brood on the past

core_teaching: When the mind's stored impressions wane, worry about past and future falls away and one meets each moment lightly and gladly.

commentaries.who: Anandabodhendra Sarasvati, Tatparya-prakasha
commentaries.gist: This is the fruit of the waning of vasanas: linking past and future comes from them, breeding aversion to past harms and craving for future gains; seeing only the present, natural bliss continues, hence 'smiling'.

commentaries.who: Context of the chapter (Mitra tr. 1891, Upashama ch. XII)
commentaries.gist: Mitra: unmindful of the past and heedless of the future, he enjoys the present with a glad heart; he did his duties while his mind stayed in contemplation.

practical_reading: Planning is fine; the trouble is the mental replay and rehearsal. Bring attention back to what is in front of you and meet it with some lightness.
misreadings: Not 'never plan'; Janaka goes on ruling a kingdom
Not forced cheerfulness
cautions: 'Smiling' should not be imposed on someone in sorrow
not_for: acute grief
someone who needs to plan urgently (debt, medical decisions)

verified_ref: Yoga Vasishtha 5.12.23 (Upashama, sarga 12). Same in Nirnaya Sagar/TP and sa.wikisource; Mitra 1891 Upashama ch. XII v.23 (Mitra's rendering is loose).
attribution_note: Vasishtha to Rama.
translation_note: Our reading matches the commentator's first, worldly sense. He also gives a spiritual sense: prajna as final realisation reaches the end of all effects (the highest goal), while delusion, entering the world of effects, destroys even the primary knowledge. Mitra paraphrases quite differently, as foresight seeing results beforehand.
context: Vasishtha praises prajna after Janaka's story: the lamp of insight dispels dullness (v.19), crosses disasters like a boat (v.20), while the dull are blown about like straw (v.21). The previous verse says the wise cross the ocean of samsara even without help or scripture. Next he says prajna should be grown first through scripture and good company, like watering a plant (v.24).

key_terms.sense: a person of insight, even without allies
reaches the end/goal of the task

core_teaching: Clear understanding is the decisive resource; it carries a task through without outside help, while poor judgment wastes even great advantages.

commentaries.who: Anandabodhendra Sarasvati, Tatparya-prakasha
commentaries.gist: In the world the person of good counsel prevails even without allies, while the foolish fall even with large armies; or, spiritually, insight reaches the goal of all aims while delusion loses even what is primary.

commentaries.who: Context of the chapter (Mitra tr. 1891, Upashama ch. XII)
commentaries.gist: Mitra frames the passage as praise of percipience: it lets one see past and future, cross dangers like a boat, and pass the world's ocean without friends or scriptures.

practical_reading: Before adding resources or people to a problem, invest in thinking it through clearly; good judgment often matters more than help.
misreadings: Not 'never ask for help'
Not contempt for people who struggle
cautions: A reader who feels they have 'ruined' something may take it as a verdict on their intelligence
not_for: someone who just failed and is blaming themselves

verified_ref: Yoga Vasishtha 5.12.26 (Upashama, sarga 12). Same in Nirnaya Sagar/TP and sa.wikisource; Mitra 1891 Upashama ch. XII v.26.
attribution_note: Vasishtha to Rama.
translation_note: Accurate. 'Purvam' (first, beforehand) carries weight: wisdom should be grown before outer gain.
context: Continuing the praise of prajna: grow it through scripture and good company like watering a sapling (v.24); a deed rooted in it bears sweet fruit in time (v.25). After this verse Vasishtha calls dullness the boundary of all sorrows and the seed of the tree of samsara, to be cut first (v.27).
core_teaching: Give at least as much effort to growing understanding as you give to earning, and give it first.

commentaries.who: Anandabodhendra Sarasvati, Tatparya-prakasha
commentaries.gist: The same kind and degree of effort is needed, no more; one need not labour beyond what one already spends on worldly gain.

commentaries.who: Context of the chapter (Mitra tr. 1891, Upashama ch. XII)
commentaries.gist: Mitra: the exertions made for outward property should first go to improving the understanding; intellectual growth should precede outward circumstances.

practical_reading: Audit your week: if hours go to career and money, set aside real, scheduled effort for reading, reflection or practice too.
misreadings: Not against earning a living
speaks_to: students choosing between grades and learning
not_for: someone in financial crisis for whom earning is urgent

verified_ref: Yoga Vasishtha 5.21.6 (Upashama, sarga 21, after the Punya-Pavana story). Same in Nirnaya Sagar/TP and sa.wikisource; Mitra 1891 Upashama ch. XXI v.6.
attribution_note: Vasishtha to Rama.
translation_note: Literal sense fine, but 'worry' narrows 'chinta'. In this chapter (on desire as bondage) the commentator reads it as dwelling on sense objects: not thinking of objects is how they are given up. Mitra likewise speaks of hankering. 'Brooding / dwelling' would fit both senses.
context: Punya and Pavana, at peace, live on in the forest and finally attain nirvana (vv.1-3). Vasishtha reflects that relatives and possessions go with no one (v.4) and that the remedy for desires is not feeding them (v.5). This verse gives the fire image. He then urges Rama to rise, look on the world with compassion, and act (v.7).

key_terms.sense: brooding grows by being brooded on
it dies by not being thought

core_teaching: Rumination and craving feed on attention; withdraw the fuel of repeated thought and they die down by themselves.

commentaries.who: Anandabodhendra Sarasvati, Tatparya-prakasha
commentaries.gist: Not thinking about sense objects is itself the way to renounce them; 'edhate' means grows.

commentaries.who: Context of the chapter (Mitra tr. 1891, Upashama ch. XXI)
commentaries.gist: Mitra: hankering after objects swells appetite as thinking swells thought, as fire grows with fuel and dies without it; suppressing appetites frees us better than fostering them.

practical_reading: When a worry or craving loops, stop arguing with it and stop feeding it; turn attention to a task or the breath and let it burn out.
misreadings: Not 'ignore real problems'
Not thought-suppression by force; the image is of not adding fuel
cautions: People with OCD or intrusive thoughts may read this as 'just don't think it'; that can backfire, so frame gently
not_for: clinical anxiety or OCD presented as a cure

verified_ref: Yoga Vasishtha 5.21.9 (Upashama, sarga 21). Same in sa.wikisource; the 1937 print (OCR) shows the verse after v.8; Mitra 1891 Upashama ch. XXI v.9.
attribution_note: Vasishtha to Rama.
translation_note: Accurate. 'Praudha-sakhi' is a mature, experienced female companion; 'dhi' is understanding. 'Sankata' is a narrow strait, a crisis.
context: Vasishtha has called the desireless state the pure 'Brahmic' state in which even a dull person is not deluded (v.8). This verse names viveka and dhi as companions. Next (v.10) he says nothing but one's own fortitude lifts one out of a crisis, and (v.11) that the mind should be raised by dispassion, scripture and greatness of spirit.
core_teaching: Discernment and clear understanding are companions you can take anywhere; with them, crises do not overwhelm you.

commentaries.who: Anandabodhendra Sarasvati, Tatparya-prakasha
commentaries.gist: Discernment is the friend; 'dhi' is understanding whose mark is awakening to the highest truth.

commentaries.who: Context of the chapter (Mitra tr. 1891, Upashama ch. XXI)
commentaries.gist: Mitra: one walking with reason as companion and understanding as consort does not fall into the hidden pitfalls along life's way.

practical_reading: In a crisis, slow down and consult your own clear judgment as you would a trusted friend before reacting.
misreadings: Not 'you don't need people'
not_for: someone in acute emergency needing outside help now

verified_ref: Yoga Vasishtha 5.21.10 (Upashama, sarga 21). Same in Nirnaya Sagar/TP and sa.wikisource; Mitra 1891 Upashama ch. XXI v.10.
attribution_note: Vasishtha to Rama.
translation_note: Defensible but contested. The two ablative compounds can describe the person in crisis (all means blocked, kin gone, as we and Mitra read it: 'bereft of property and friends'). Anandabodhendra instead reads them actively: one who has himself given up all wealth and pushed relatives away by cutting inner attachment, i.e. the renouncer's own fortitude. Mitra also adds 'and reliance in God', which is not in the Sanskrit.
context: Following v.9 on discernment as a friend, Vasishtha says only one's own steadiness (dhairya) lifts one from crisis. Next he says one should raise one's own mind by dispassion, scripture and greatness of spirit (v.11), and that no wealth gives what greatness of mind gives (v.12).

key_terms.sense: with all means/wealth shut off (or: having renounced all wealth)
with kin pushed away / let go

core_teaching: In the end it is one's own inner steadiness that carries one through a crisis; outer supports are not the final resource.

commentaries.who: Anandabodhendra Sarasvati, Tatparya-prakasha
commentaries.gist: The compounds describe one who has given up all wealth and, by severing inner attachment, pushed kin aside as with a hand; such a person's own fortitude raises himself out of crisis.

commentaries.who: Context of the chapter (Mitra tr. 1891, Upashama ch. XXI)
commentaries.gist: Mitra: when bereft of property and friends, one has no help in adversity but one's own patience and reliance on God; the next verses urge elevating the mind by learning and dispassion.

practical_reading: When outside help runs out, draw on your own steadiness: one small decision, one next step. Accepting help when it comes is not a failure of this.
misreadings: Not 'go it alone' or 'don't ask for help'
Not a praise of cutting off family
cautions: Can deepen isolation for someone already abandoned; pair with the reminder that help is welcome
The commentator's reading (pushing relatives away) should not be presented to a family-estranged reader as an ideal
speaks_to: someone whose support has fallen away
job loss with no safety net
immigrants or people far from family
not_for: suicidal crisis (needs outside help, not self-reliance)
abuse situations where reaching out is vital

verified_ref: Yoga Vasishtha 5.21.14 (Upashama, sarga 21). Same in Nirnaya Sagar/TP and sa.wikisource; Mitra 1891 Upashama ch. XXI v.14.
attribution_note: Vasishtha to Rama.
translation_note: Accurate. 'Purna' (full) in context means full through desirelessness: the next verse says the mind becomes full by dispassion, not by following desire.
context: Vasishtha has said greatness of mind gives what no wealth can (v.12) and that those tossed up and down by desire have minds always feverish (v.13). This verse gives the shoe image. Next: the mind becomes full through dispassion and empty through desire (v.15), and craving dries the heart like Agastya drinking the ocean (v.16).

key_terms.sense: when the mind is full, complete
for one whose feet are covered by shoes
the earth is as if covered with leather

core_teaching: Change the mind rather than trying to change the whole world; a mind that is whole finds the world sweet, as a shod foot finds every road smooth.

commentaries.who: Anandabodhendra Sarasvati, Tatparya-prakasha
commentaries.gist: All three kinds of suffering are rooted in faults of mind; when the mind is filled with the nectar of Brahman, the whole world appears full of bliss, just as the ground seems leather-covered to one wearing soft shoes.

commentaries.who: Context of the chapter (Mitra tr. 1891, Upashama ch. XXI)
commentaries.gist: Mitra: a mind full of knowledge finds the world filled with ambrosia and moves over it easily, like one walking in shoes; desirelessness fills the mind more than fulfilled desires.

practical_reading: Instead of waiting for every person and circumstance to change, work on the inner 'shoes': contentment, perspective, less craving.
misreadings: Not 'outer problems don't matter' or a reason to ignore injustice
cautions: Can sound like blaming someone's mind for real external harm (abuse, discrimination)
speaks_to: chronic irritation with people and circumstances
not_for: someone suffering abuse or injustice that needs to be addressed outwardly

verified_ref: Yoga Vasishtha 5.24.19 (Upashama, sarga 24, Bali's story). Same in Nirnaya Sagar/TP and sa.wikisource. Mitra 1891 (Upashama ch. XXIV) paraphrases freely and his verse numbers do not align here (the idea appears around his v.40).
attribution_note: Virochana to his son Bali (recalled by Bali), within Vasishtha's narration. Correct.
translation_note: Accurate, but 'this' needs its referent: eṣā is the 'yukti' of v.17-18, complete disinterest (anāstha) in all sense objects, the means by which the elephant of the mind is tamed. Our note's 'mastering the mind' is the goal; the thing hard and easy to attain is dispassion toward objects.
context: Virochana tells Bali that the world is a transformation of the mind and that conquering it conquers all (vv.14-15). Bali asks for the method (v.16). Virochana: total disinterest in sense objects is the supreme method that tames the mind (vv.17-18). This verse adds that it is hard unpractised and easy when practised; it grows step by step like a watered creeper (v.20) and cannot be had by wishing, as rice cannot grow unsown (v.21).

key_terms.sense: extremely hard and also easy to reach
disinterest in sense objects, the thing referred to

core_teaching: Dispassion is not a gift you either have or lack: practice turns what seems impossible into something natural.

commentaries.who: Anandabodhendra Sarasvati, Tatparya-prakasha
commentaries.gist: Glosses the surrounding verses: anāstha means non-craving and yukti means the method; the creeper image shows it widens and becomes evident with practice, and 'shathatman' is the mind greedy for pleasure, which cannot get it without practice.

commentaries.who: Context of the chapter (Mitra tr. 1891, Upashama ch. XXIV)
commentaries.gist: Mitra: it is hard to get rid of serpentine desires without continued practice of indifference to worldly affairs; Bali then asks how such indifference takes root.

practical_reading: Whatever inner change you are attempting, expect it to feel impossible at first; repeat it daily and it becomes easy.
misreadings: Not 'it's easy, so you're failing if it's hard'
not_for: someone who has been practising hard and feels blamed for not progressing

verified_ref: Yoga Vasishtha 5.31.35 (Upashama, sarga 31, start of Prahlada's story). Same in Nirnaya Sagar/TP and sa.wikisource; Mitra 1891 Upashama ch. XXXI v.35.
attribution_note: Prahlada reflecting to himself, in Vasishtha's narration. Correct.
translation_note: Accurate. Note the motive in context: Prahlada first sees surrender to Hari as the only 'remedy' against an unbeatable foe (v.34); devotion begins as a strategy and ripens later.
context: Hiranyakashipu has been killed by Vishnu as the man-lion and the demons are routed. Prahlada reflects that Hari cannot be beaten by weapons and has outlasted all their past wars (vv.30-33), so the only way to 'overcome' him is to take refuge in him (v.34). This verse states that resolve; next he calls Hari the cause of creation and dissolution (v.36) and vows refuge (v.37).

key_terms.sense: with all the force of my striving

core_teaching: When every other way is closed, complete, wholehearted refuge in God is the way through.

commentaries.who: Anandabodhendra Sarasvati, Tatparya-prakasha
commentaries.gist: With one's whole nature, every kind of understanding and every effort and undertaking, he alone is the refuge for those seeking shelter; there is no other way.

commentaries.who: Context of the chapter (Mitra tr. 1891, Upashama ch. XXXI)
commentaries.gist: Mitra: Prahlada, having found one expedient against Hari's might, resolves to have recourse to him with full contrition, as the true refuge and only resort of all.

practical_reading: When you have tried everything and are cornered, wholehearted surrender, putting your whole mind and effort into trust rather than resistance, can open a new way.
misreadings: Not passivity; the verse asks for all of one's effort turned in one direction
cautions: Speaks from defeat and the death of a parent (Prahlada's father has just been killed); can be strong for someone at rock bottom
not_for: readers uncomfortable with theistic devotion (the verse names God)

verified_ref: Yoga Vasishtha 5.31.37 (Upashama, sarga 31). Same in Nirnaya Sagar/TP and sa.wikisource; Mitra 1891 Upashama ch. XXXI v.37.
attribution_note: Prahlada to himself. Correct.
translation_note: Accurate. 'Samprapanno 'smi' is 'I have taken refuge' (prapatti). 'Narayana-mayo hy aham' could also be 'I am made of Narayana'; v.39 goes further: 'I am Hari'.
context: Following his resolve (v.35) and praise of Hari as cause of all (v.36), Prahlada makes this vow. Then he names the mantra that never leaves his heart (v.38), declares 'Hari is the sky, earth, world; I am Hari, full of Vishnu' (v.39), and says one should worship Vishnu by becoming Vishnu (v.40).
core_teaching: Refuge is a decision made in a moment and then lived always and everywhere, until one feels filled by the divine.

commentaries.who: Anandabodhendra Sarasvati, Tatparya-prakasha
commentaries.gist: Having decided, he resolves on surrender with his whole being; asked whether he takes refuge only in some place or time, he answers: everywhere, being full of Narayana in all places, times and things.

commentaries.who: Context of the chapter (Mitra tr. 1891, Upashama ch. XXXI)
commentaries.gist: Mitra: from this moment he will think only of the unborn Narayana and rely on him, who is present everywhere and full in himself.

practical_reading: Turning points can be chosen: 'from today' you can begin a practice of trust and remembrance and let it grow into every hour.
misreadings: Not a one-time ritual; it is a lifelong orientation
speaks_to: someone who has been running from faith
not_for: non-theistic readers

verified_ref: Yoga Vasishtha 5.31.38 (Upashama, sarga 31). Same in Nirnaya Sagar/TP and sa.wikisource; Mitra 1891 Upashama ch. XXXI v.38.
attribution_note: Prahlada to himself. Correct.
translation_note: Accurate. 'Sarvartha-sadhaka' is 'accomplishing every aim'. Our misuse note is apt.
context: Directly after vowing refuge (v.37). He then identifies himself with Hari (v.39) and states that a non-Vishnu worshipping Vishnu gains no fruit; one must worship Vishnu as Vishnu (v.40), which ends the chapter. In the following chapters he worships in his shrine and mind until Vishnu appears.

key_terms.sense: from the chamber of the heart

core_teaching: A short prayer held continuously in the heart becomes as natural as air in the sky.

commentaries.who: Anandabodhendra Sarasvati, Tatparya-prakasha
commentaries.gist: He resolves on continuous japa of this Vedic mantra; it is taken without 'Om' because the form with pranava needs a pure place and is not for unbroken repetition; 'from the heart' marks mental japa as primary.

commentaries.who: Context of the chapter (Mitra tr. 1891, Upashama ch. XXXI)
commentaries.gist: Mitra: obeisance to Narayana is his faith for success in all undertakings, and he prays it may abide in his heart as wind in empty air.

practical_reading: Keep one short prayer or name in the mind through the day, silently, while walking or working; it steadies the heart.
misreadings: 'Every aim' is praise of the name, not a promise of particular outcomes
cautions: Commentator's point that the mantra without Om suits continuous silent repetition is useful practical guidance
speaks_to: people who find long prayers hard
not_for: non-Vaishnava or non-theistic readers without adaptation

verified_ref: Yoga Vasishtha 5.33.19 (Upashama, sarga 33). Same in Nirnaya Sagar/TP and sa.wikisource; Mitra 1891 Upashama ch. XXXIII v.19.
attribution_note: Prahlada to Vishnu, who has appeared in his shrine (vv.16-18). Correct.
translation_note: Accurate. A pushpitagra-metre hymn verse; each later verse of the hymn ends with 'prapadye'.
context: Prahlada worships Vishnu inwardly and in his shrine until the demons of his city also turn devotee and the gods are astonished (ch.32-33). Vishnu reassures the gods and comes through the underworld to Prahlada's shrine (vv.16-17). Prahlada, overjoyed, sings this hymn, which continues with Hari's beauty and attributes.
core_teaching: God is the shelter of exactly those who have no other shelter; the devotee approaches with that trust.

commentaries.who: Anandabodhendra Sarasvati, Tatparya-prakasha
commentaries.gist: Treasure-house because the three worlds are kept safe within him; remover of inner and outer darkness; self-luminous light beyond sun and moon; protector of those with no other refuge; called unborn, unfailing and Lord in relation to the three gunas.

commentaries.who: Context of the chapter (Mitra tr. 1891, Upashama ch. XXXIII)
commentaries.gist: Mitra: Prahlada adores Hari, unborn and undecaying, receptacle of the three worlds, dispeller of darkness, refuge of the helpless and friendless.

practical_reading: When you feel you have nowhere to turn, this is a prayer for exactly that state.
speaks_to: guilt and shame ('remover of every stain')
not_for: non-theistic readers

verified_ref: Yoga Vasishtha 5.36.1 (Upashama, sarga 36, opening). Same in Nirnaya Sagar/TP and sa.wikisource; Mitra 1891 Upashama ch. XXXVI v.1 ('Hymn to the Soul').
attribution_note: Prahlada, addressing the Self as Lord. Correct.
translation_note: Accurate. 'Sarva-padatita' is 'beyond every word/state/category'; 'samsmriti' is recollection. Mitra renders it loosely ('art found in myself by my good fortune').
context: Through chs.34-35 Prahlada inquires into the Self, realises it and passes beyond his old ego, saying his great dangers are gone. Ch.36 opens with this greeting. He goes on: who else is a friend in the three worlds (v.2); you were near all along, yet far by many births (v.5); salutations to you who are Shiva, Vishnu, Brahma and all.

key_terms.sense: after long, come back to memory
by good fortune you are found

core_teaching: Realisation is described as remembering, not acquiring: the Self was always there and is now recognised, greeted like an old friend and as the Lord.

commentaries.who: Context of the chapter (Mitra tr. 1891, Upashama ch. XXXVI)
commentaries.gist: Mitra titles it a hymn to the Soul: Prahlada thanks the Lord beyond all things found within himself, calls him his only friend, present everywhere, long distant and now near.

commentaries.who: Anandabodhendra Sarasvati, Tatparya-prakasha (on the end of ch.35)
commentaries.gist: Glosses Prahlada's state just before: he marvels at his former ego as at a dream after waking; his mind, now of the form of boundless Brahman, has shed the cloud of 'I'; all great calamities are gone.

practical_reading: Moments of deep peace can feel like coming home to something you had forgotten; treat them as remembering who you are.
misreadings: Not self-worship in an ego sense; the 'I' that is greeted is beyond the ego
speaks_to: returning to faith after a long gap
not_for: readers in acute distress (abstract)
research_note: Anandabodhendra's gloss on 36.1 itself could not be isolated in the OCR; the second note is his comment on the verses immediately before it.

verified_ref: Yoga Vasishtha 5.41.3 (Upashama, sarga 41, 'Prahlada's installation'). Same in Nirnaya Sagar/TP and sa.wikisource; Mitra 1891 Upashama ch. XLI v.3.
attribution_note: Prahlada to Vishnu, after Vishnu has roused him from samadhi with his conch and words (ch.38-40). Our 'prasang' field is null for this verse; it belongs to the Prahlada prasang.
translation_note: Accurate. The commentator says the fatigue came from deliberating what benefits the asuras and harms the gods, i.e. political scheming of his old life, and that he says 'a moment' because in samadhi the length of time is not felt (he had been absorbed a very long time). Mitra reads it as cares for his people's weal and woe.
context: Prahlada sat in samadhi so long that his kingdom fell into disorder (ch.37). Vishnu comes, wakes him and asks him to live liberated and rule (chs.38-40). Prahlada speaks for the first time: this verse, then 'by your grace I am settled; in samadhi or out of it I am the same' (v.4). He is then installed as king.

key_terms.sense: weighing what helps and what harms
I have come to rest for a moment

core_teaching: Endless calculation and duty exhaust the mind; rest in the Self heals it, and that rest feels brief even when long.

commentaries.who: Anandabodhendra Sarasvati, Tatparya-prakasha
commentaries.gist: He was wearied by weighing what helps the asuras and hurts the gods; 'a moment' is said because in samadhi one does not register the length of time.

commentaries.who: Context of the chapter (Mitra tr. 1891, Upashama ch. XLI)
commentaries.gist: Mitra: Lord, I was much tired with many state affairs and thoughts of my people's weal and woe, and have now found a little rest from my labour.

practical_reading: If decision fatigue and responsibility have worn you out, real inner rest, not just distraction, is what restores you, and it can be found even briefly.
misreadings: Not a call to abandon responsibilities; Vishnu sends him back to rule
speaks_to: managers and carers with decision fatigue
research_note: prasang is null in our data.

verified_ref: Yoga Vasishtha 5.41.4 (Upashama, sarga 41). Same in Nirnaya Sagar/TP and sa.wikisource; Mitra 1891 Upashama ch. XLI v.4.
attribution_note: Prahlada to Vishnu. Correct.
translation_note: Accurate. 'Rupena' means 'in my real nature'. The commentator adds that he is the same in samadhi and out of it, and also in embodied and disembodied liberation.
context: Straight after v.3. Prahlada continues: I have seen you within for long with a pure mind, and now see you outside too (v.5); I was in that boundless vision not from grief, delusion, or fear of the world (v.7); where the One exists there is no sorrow or loss (v.8). Vishnu then installs him as king.

key_terms.sense: a right, settled state has come
in absorption and out of it

core_teaching: True steadiness does not depend on being in meditation; it continues through ordinary life.

commentaries.who: Anandabodhendra Sarasvati, Tatparya-prakasha
commentaries.gist: 'Sthiti' is abiding in one's own nature through knowledge of truth; 'rupena' is the absolute nature; he is the same in samadhi and outside it, and in embodied and bodiless liberation.

commentaries.who: Context of the chapter (Mitra tr. 1891, Upashama ch. XLI)
commentaries.gist: Mitra: by thy grace I am settled in myself, and in trance or waking I enjoy tranquillity of mind at all times.

practical_reading: Aim for the calm of practice to carry into the rest of the day: the test of meditation is how you are afterwards.
misreadings: Not 'I no longer need practice'
speaks_to: meditators whose calm vanishes at work
not_for: someone who feels guilty that their calm doesn't last

verified_ref: Yoga Vasishtha 5.43.9 (Upashama, sarga 43). Same in Nirnaya Sagar/TP and sa.wikisource; Mitra 1891 Upashama ch. XLIII v.9.
attribution_note: Vasishtha answering Rama's objection (v.3). Correct.
translation_note: Accurate. Our 'line' ('Both are real paths') is fair, but the chapter ranks them: self-inquiry is primary (mukhya), boons and grace secondary (gauna) (v.11). The commentator reads even the grace route as won by one's own effort of devotion.
context: Rama asks: if everything is won by effort, how did Prahlada wake only by Vishnu's boon (v.3)? Vasishtha: Prahlada earned it himself; the Self and Narayana are one, like sesame and its oil (vv.4-8). This verse gives two routes. Next: even long-pleased, Madhava cannot give knowledge to one who does not inquire (v.10); inquiry from effort is the main cause, boons secondary (v.11).

key_terms.sense: the Self wakes by itself, by its own power

core_teaching: Awakening can come by one's own inquiry or through God reached in devotion; in this chapter both are finally one's own effort, since Vishnu and the Self are not two.

commentaries.who: Anandabodhendra Sarasvati, Tatparya-prakasha
commentaries.gist: 'By its own power' means by the strength of inquiry made through one's own effort; 'through Vishnu's body' means via the effort that takes the form of devotion.

commentaries.who: Context of the chapter (Mitra tr. 1891, Upashama ch. XLIII)
commentaries.gist: Mitra: sometimes the soul wakes by its own intuition, sometimes by the grace of the personal Vishnu through faith; but the god, however pleased, cannot give knowledge to one without reasoning.

practical_reading: Whether you lean on prayer or on reflection, the work of seeing clearly is still yours; grace and effort meet in the same place.
misreadings: Not that grace is irrelevant
Not that devotion is lesser for everyone; but the chapter does rank inquiry first
cautions: Devotional readers may be uncomfortable with the chapter's ranking; use the verse with the effort-and-grace framing
speaks_to: devotees who also want to think

verified_ref: Yoga Vasishtha 5.43.25 (Upashama, sarga 43). Same in Nirnaya Sagar/TP and sa.wikisource; Mitra 1891 Upashama ch. XLIII v.25.
attribution_note: Vasishtha to Rama. Correct.
translation_note: Accurate. Our misuse note ('not a dismissal of prayer') is good guidance for readers, but softer than the context, which is openly polemical against external worship (see context). The commentator only supplies an implied 'as'.
context: Vasishtha is in a sharp passage: Vaishnava devotion was devised for those who flee scripture, effort and inquiry (v.20); worship is the secondary method when practice is lacking (v.21); win your own mind or you are a 'forest donkey' (v.24). After this verse: Vishnu dwells within every person and those who leave him to seek an outer Vishnu are low (v.26); the conch-bearing form is secondary (v.27).
core_teaching: Give your own mind the same loving, patient appeal you give the gods; winning it over is the real work.

commentaries.who: Anandabodhendra Sarasvati, Tatparya-prakasha
commentaries.gist: Supplies only the implied comparison: just as entreaty is made to Madhava, so it should be made to one's own mind.

commentaries.who: Context of the chapter (Mitra tr. 1891, Upashama ch. XLIII)
commentaries.gist: Mitra: people seek favour from gods and great men but not from their own hearts, which can give every blessing; the next verse places Vishnu within every person.

practical_reading: Talk to your own mind kindly and persistently, as you would pray: ask it to settle, to let go, to choose well.
misreadings: Not 'prayer is useless'
Not 'worship yourself'
cautions: The surrounding verses disparage image worship and call devotion a device for those who avoid effort; avoid quoting them in a devotional plan
speaks_to: people who pray but neglect inner work
not_for: strongly devotional readers if presented with its polemical context

verified_ref: Yoga Vasishtha 5.43.32 (Upashama, sarga 43). Same in Nirnaya Sagar/TP and sa.wikisource; Mitra 1891 Upashama ch. XLIII v.32.
attribution_note: Vasishtha to Rama. Correct.
translation_note: Accurate. 'Ashu' (soon) and 'shanaih shanaih' (slowly) sit together; the commentator says 'soon' stresses that clarity surely comes. 'Sahakara' is a fragrant, fully ripe mango.
context: Vasishtha softens: one who lacks self-discernment should worship the four-armed Lord, and by that worship and austerity the mind becomes pure in time (vv.30-31). This verse: daily practice and discernment clear the mind, as a mango ripens. Next: so by the occasion of Hari's worship the Self gains the fruit by itself (v.33).

key_terms.sense: the state of a ripe, fragrant mango

core_teaching: Clarity is a ripening: steady daily practice plus discernment surely brings it, gradually and naturally.

commentaries.who: Anandabodhendra Sarasvati, Tatparya-prakasha
commentaries.gist: 'Soon' signals that clarity is certain to come; 'sahakara' names the state of the mango when its flower and fruit are most fragrant.

commentaries.who: Context of the chapter (Mitra tr. 1891, Upashama ch. XLIII)
commentaries.gist: Mitra: daily practice of self-control and meditation purifies the mind, which like the mango gains its virtues one by one; worship of Hari can likewise lead there.

practical_reading: Do the small practice every day and stop checking whether you are 'there yet'; ripening happens on its own schedule.
misreadings: Not 'it will be quick'

verified_ref: Yoga Vasishtha 5.61.2 (Upashama, sarga 61, after Suraghu's story; the chapter opens the Suraghu-Parigha dialogue). Same in Nirnaya Sagar/TP and sa.wikisource; Mitra 1891 Upashama ch. LXI v.2 (Mitra vol. 3).
attribution_note: Vasishtha to Rama. Our 'prasang' is null; it belongs to Suraghu's story (Upashama 55-61).
translation_note: Accurate. 'Etam drishtim' refers back to v.1: relying, like Suraghu, on the sole reality of the one Self to remove sin and sorrow. The commentator glosses the child 'having gained light'.
context: King Suraghu of the Kiratas, troubled by the duty to punish and reward, is taught by the sage Mandavya and settles in the vision of the one Self (chs.55-60). Vasishtha urges Rama to do likewise (v.1). This verse: holding that view, the mind no longer burns. Next: discernment brings relief like grabbing a firm tuft of grass while falling into a pit (v.3); then the story of Suraghu and his friend Parigha begins.

key_terms.sense: the mind does not burn with distress
a child who has been given a lamp

core_teaching: Seeing life from the vision of the one Self removes the mind's burning, as light removes a child's terror of the dark.

commentaries.who: Anandabodhendra Sarasvati, Tatparya-prakasha
commentaries.gist: Sin is reversed when knowledge of truth uproots it; the child, having obtained light, no longer suffers; the chapter tells of Suraghu's meeting with Parigha.

commentaries.who: Context of the chapter (Mitra tr. 1891, Upashama ch. LXI)

core_teaching: Knowledge should not puff up the mind; humility in learning is another of Bhushunda's keys to a long, sound life.

practical_reading: Each time you learn or achieve something, notice any swagger, and let it turn into curiosity instead.
misreadings: Not anti-intellectual

key_terms.sense: sad when a person is sad

core_teaching: Sharing others' joys and sorrows and being a friend to all is part of a healthy life; Bhushunda pairs it next with steadiness in adversity (v.35).

commentaries.who: Anandabodhendra Sarasvati, Tatparya-prakasha

commentaries.who: Context of the chapter (Mitra tr. 1891, Nirvana ch. XXVI)
commentaries.gist: Mitra: he is happy at others' happiness and sorry at their misery, and this universal fellow-feeling keeps him alive and fresh.

practical_reading: Let yourself be glad for others' good news and moved by their trouble; friendship and fellow-feeling are good for you too.
misreadings: Not a call to absorb everyone's pain without limits

attribution_note: Vasishtha to Shiva (retold to Rama). The verse grammatically continues v.107 ('for those blessed with remembrance of the three-eyed one, O Maheshvara...').
translation_note: Accurate. 'Parighurnita' is 'whirling, swaying' (with joy). Mitra includes v.107's phrase about remembering the three-eyed god.
context: Vasishtha recalls to Rama how, living as an ascetic on Kailasa, Shiva and Parvati came to him; he worshipped them, and Shiva asked whether his austerities were unhindered and his fears quieted (vv.95-106). Vasishtha replies in vv.107-113 praising remembrance of Shiva. He then asks Shiva how God should truly be worshipped, which leads to Shiva's teaching on inner worship.

key_terms.sense: nothing at all is hard to reach
of those whose minds whirl/are steeped (in it)

core_teaching: For one whose mind is absorbed in the joy of remembering God, nothing seems out of reach and fear loses its hold.

commentaries.who: Anandabodhendra Sarasvati, Tatparya-prakasha
commentaries.gist: Glosses the frame: Vasishtha answers with humble, conciliating speech; v.108 itself is left without comment, and v.109 is read as praise that there is no being who does not bow to Shiva.

commentaries.who: Context of the chapter (Mitra tr. 1891, Nirvana ch. XXIX)
commentaries.gist: Mitra: nothing is unattainable and nothing to be feared for one who remembers the three-eyed god always and whose heart is filled with rapture by that remembrance.

practical_reading: When fear rises, deliberately turn the mind to what you love and trust most; remembrance itself steadies you.
misreadings: Not a promise that hardship will not come
cautions: 'Nothing is hard to reach' can sound like a guarantee; frame as the felt confidence of devotion
not_for: non-theistic readers

verified_ref: Yoga Vasishtha 6a.29.111-112 as numbered in sa.wikisource and the Nirnaya Sagar text; but the sentence actually runs 6a.29.110b-113a. Mitra 1891 Nirvana ch. XXIX vv.110-113.
attribution_note: Vasishtha to Shiva. Correct.
translation_note: Incomplete sentence. 'Tanoti caishyato bijam' completes v.110b: remembering you is the fruit of past merit, the watering of present merit, and sows the seed of future merit (the commentator: of what is yet to be done). Our translation ends 'Holding the great wish-jewel of remembering you, I...'; the sentence finishes in v.113a: '...I have set my foot on the head of all calamities' (the commentator: present and future ones). context: Part of Vasishtha's reply to Shiva's enquiry after his welfare (vv.107-113), praising smarana. Immediately after, he asks Shiva his doubt about true worship, and Shiva teaches that the real God is consciousness itself and real worship is inner.

key_terms.sense: and spreads the seed of what is to come
the one jar of wisdom's nectar
the gate of the city of liberation
a foot set on the head of all calamities

core_teaching: Remembrance of God links past, present and future merit, holds wisdom and steadiness, opens the door to freedom, and puts the devotee above calamity.

commentaries.who: Anandabodhendra Sarasvati, Tatparya-prakasha
commentaries.gist: Remembrance is the fruit of merit cultivated earlier, waters present merit and sows the seed for what is still to be done; 'all calamities' means present and future ones.

commentaries.who: Context of the chapter (Mitra tr. 1891, Nirvana ch. XXIX)
commentaries.gist: Mitra: remembrance brings the reward of past lives' merit and waters the present; it is the jar of knowledge's nectar, the gateway to salvation, a priceless gem, and it tramples all calamities.

practical_reading: A habit of remembering the divine is cumulative: it grows from past practice, nourishes today and prepares tomorrow.
misreadings: Not a guarantee against misfortune; it is about standing above it
cautions: Translation currently trails off; fix before use
speaks_to: those building a daily remembrance habit
not_for: non-theistic readers

verified_ref: Yoga Vasishtha 6a.39.2 (Nirvana, first half, sarga 39, inner worship). Same in Nirnaya Sagar/TP (Motilal reprint) and sa.wikisource; Mitra 1891 Nirvana ch. XXXIX v.2.
attribution_note: Shiva (Ishvara) to Vasishtha. Correct.
translation_note: Accurate. 'Sarvacara-gata' is 'running through all conduct'; the commentator glosses it as pervading all activities. 'Dhyanatmika' is 'made of meditation'.
context: Shiva has taught that the true deity is consciousness, present in everything (ch.38). Here he begins the inner worship: the purest of purifiers, destroying all darkness (v.1); it goes on in every state (v.2); one should constantly meditate on Shiva dwelling in the body as one's own Self, the cause of all perception (v.3), whether lying, rising, walking or standing (v.4).

key_terms.sense: worship that runs through all conduct

core_teaching: The highest worship needs no special place or time: it is continuous inner attention to the divine as one's own awareness, carried into every activity.

commentaries.who: Anandabodhendra Sarasvati, Tatparya-prakasha
commentaries.gist: The chapter describes the inner worship of Shiva as the inner Self; it destroys all ignorance, and in v.2 'gata' means it accompanies every kind of activity.

commentaries.who: Context of the chapter (Mitra tr. 1891, Nirvana ch. XXXIX)
commentaries.gist: Mitra: this inward worship rests on mental meditation and goes on in every state, sitting or walking, waking or sleeping, worshipping Shiva in the body in spirit.

practical_reading: You don't need a shrine to worship; bring quiet attention to the presence within while you commute, work, cook or lie down.
misreadings: Not a rejection of temple worship; Shiva also describes outer worship elsewhere
speaks_to: busy people who can't keep long rituals

attribution_note: Kumbha (Chudala in disguise) to King Shikhidhvaja. Correct. Our setting is incomplete: see context.
translation_note: Accurate. 'Utajadi-shosha' is the drying up/destruction of the hut and the rest; Mitra reads it as burning his hut and chattels (he has just burnt them).
context: SENSITIVE CONTEXT. Urged by Kumbha that he has not truly renounced, Shikhidhvaja burns his hut and belongings (vv.1-11). Told he still has not given up everything, he decides his body is what remains and rises to hurl it off a cliff (vv.15-17). Kumbha stops him: the body is innocent, a dumb tool moved by something else; destroying it is not renunciation (vv.18-27). He asks what then moves the body (v.28); this verse answers: not giving up body, kingdom or hut. The answer that follows is the mind (vv.30-43).

key_terms.sense: not by giving up (destroying) the body
not by wrecking the hut and the rest

core_teaching: Real letting go is not done by destroying the body or abandoning outer life; it is the mind that must be released.

commentaries.who: Anandabodhendra Sarasvati, Tatparya-prakasha
commentaries.gist: The body is not the offender; the ego that agitates it is. Renouncing by throwing away the body cannot succeed, since a body fit for knowledge is rare, and the root of birth and action regrows.

commentaries.who: Context of the chapter (Mitra tr. 1891, Nirvana ch. LXXXXIII)
commentaries.gist: Mitra: Kumbha interrupts the prince as he goes to dash his body from the crag, calls the body innocent and harmless, and says neither forsaking realm, body nor burning hut and chattels makes renunciation of all.

practical_reading: Dramatic outer changes, quitting, leaving, punishing yourself, do not by themselves bring peace; the work is with the mind that drives them.
misreadings: Not 'never change your life'
Not a dismissal of genuine renunciation; it relocates it to the mind
cautions: The verse answers a man about to throw himself from a cliff. Never use it lightly or with imagery of falling; if used for someone with thoughts of self-harm, the message must be explicitly protective (the body is innocent; do not harm it) and paired with crisis resources
Our setting line omits the suicide attempt; an editor must know it
speaks_to: someone who wants to escape their life (quit, move, cut off everyone) to find peace
not_for: a reader in active suicidal crisis without professional support framing

Shikhidhvaja's awakening follows in later chapters, and he finally returns with Chudala to rule.

key_terms.sense: best of those who know renunciation

core_teaching: To renounce the mind's grasping is to renounce everything; when that is done, reality is directly known.

commentaries.who: Anandabodhendra Sarasvati, Tatparya-prakasha
commentaries.gist: Giving up the mind makes total renunciation possible, failing which it is impossible; once achieved, the supreme reality of boundless bliss is experienced.

commentaries.who: Context of the chapter (Mitra tr. 1891, Nirvana ch. LXXXXIII)
commentaries.gist: Mitra: resignation of the mind is what makes renunciation of all; succeed in that and you know the truth and the true felicity of the soul.

practical_reading: Instead of asking what to give up outwardly, ask what your mind is clinging to; letting that go is the real renunciation.
misreadings: Not 'stop thinking' or numbness
cautions: Same scene as 6a.93.29 (attempted self-destruction just before)
speaks_to: people considering monastic or radical life changes

core_teaching: Great action is timely, fitting and unattached: do what the moment requires without clinging to it.

commentaries.who: Anandabodhendra Sarasvati, Tatparya-prakasha
commentaries.gist: Glosses the great doer's conduct as in keeping with the world's ways; the following verse means one who, firm in the Self, stays even toward prescribed and forbidden action.

commentaries.who: Context of the chapter (Mitra tr. 1891, Nirvana ch. CXV)
commentaries.gist: Mitra: he does his duties best who has his wits ready at the fittest time and sits unconcerned at other times like a silent sage.

practical_reading: Do the right thing at the right time in the way the task needs, then put it down; don't carry it around afterwards.
misreadings: Not detachment as not caring about quality

attribution_note: Shiva to Bhringisha. Correct.
translation_note: Accurate. The commentator: he takes them in with an equal attitude, as experience. Our note's echo of Gita 2.70 (ocean filled by rivers) is a fair parallel but our own.
context: Among the definitions of the 'great enjoyer' (vv.21-33): one who hates nothing and craves nothing but enjoys what comes (v.21), watches the world as a witness (v.23). key_terms.sense: as the ocean takes in waters

core_teaching: The 'great enjoyer' is large enough to receive big joys and big sorrows without being overturned, as the ocean takes in every river.

commentaries.who: Anandabodhendra Sarasvati, Tatparya-prakasha
commentaries.gist: He receives joys and sorrows with an even attitude, for experience; in v.25 old age, death and poverty are 'delightful' because seen as Brahman.

commentaries.who: Context of the chapter (Mitra tr. 1891, Nirvana ch. CXV)
commentaries.gist: Mitra: he is the man of greatest gratification who bears all ups and downs of fortune with equal fortitude, as the deep sea holds its waves.

practical_reading: Let life's highs and lows flow in without being swept away; you can feel them fully and still remain yourself.
misreadings: Not emotional numbness

context: After Shiva's three definitions, Vasishtha tells Rama to stand in this view, free of fever (v.40), contemplate Brahman as ever-risen and pure with nothing else besides (vv.41-42), and closes the chapter with this verse on acting outwardly while turned inward.
core_teaching: Inner anchoring makes outer work sustainable: act fully in the world while resting inward, and weariness and ego both fall away.

verified_ref: Yoga Vasishtha 6b.44.32 (Nirvana, second half, sarga 44). Same in sa.wikisource (marked 6.2.44) and the Nirnaya Sagar/TP text; Mitra 1891 Nirvana (Uttarardha) ch. XLIV v.32 (Mitra vol. 4).
attribution_note: Vasishtha to Rama (answering Rama's request in v.1 to describe the tree of samadhi). Our 'prasang' is null.
translation_note: Accurate. 'Its' (yasyam, feminine) refers to the cool shade/coolness of the tree of discernment in v.31; the commentator glosses it as 'in which shade'. 'Avantara' is the wild stretches of worldly life; 'kolahala' the commentator reads as the din of many disputing doctrines.
context: Rama asks Vasishtha to describe the tree of samadhi with its creepers and flowers (v.1). Vasishtha describes it: its creepers are clarity, truth, steadiness, equanimity, peace, friendliness, compassion (v.23); it cools the directions like a rain cloud (v.27); as the tree of discernment grows in the heart's forest it spreads shade and coolness (vv.30-31). This verse: the tired mind-deer rests there. The rest of the chapter describes that deer's long, hunted wanderings.

key_terms.sense: worn out in the wilds along the way
a traveller worn out since birth
harried by noise on the road

core_teaching: The restless, hunted mind finds its rest in the cool shade of discernment and meditation, as a lifelong traveller finally rests.

commentaries.who: Anandabodhendra Sarasvati, Tatparya-prakasha
commentaries.gist: The mind-deer, wearied in the wilderness tracts of samsara, rests in that shade; the following verses detail its many causes of exhaustion; even on a good path it is thrown off by the clamour of disputants.

commentaries.who: Context of the chapter (Mitra tr. 1891, Nirvana ch. XLIV)
commentaries.gist: Mitra: the deer-like mind, tired of wandering the world's deserts, rests under this cool shade like a traveller worn out from birth; it is hunted by the passions and chases the mirage of ego.

practical_reading: If your mind feels like it has been running all its life, give it a daily place of shade: a few minutes of stillness and reflection.
cautions: Later verses describe the deer hunted and falling into a pit; use only this verse's restful image
